Starting from thickness or from the thermal pad inverts it, and delegating aperture sizing to the supplier skips the engineering decision.

prompt: Why is a QFN thermal pad usually segmented rather than printed as one large opening?

options.text: Segmentation raises the area ratio of the thermal pad so that paste releases cleanly.
Segmentation is required because a single pad cannot be covered by a laser-cut foil.
Segmentation controls paste volume and gives gas a path out during reflow.
Segmentation reduces the thermal performance of the joint to a level the paste allows.

explanation: The lesson describes segmenting or reducing the centre pad to control paste volume and allow gas to escape, which prevents voiding and lift. Segmentation does affect the ratio indirectly, but that is not the reason given; laser cutting has no such limitation; and the aim is a sound joint, not a deliberately worse thermal path.

prompt: For chip components the lesson gives a starting band for aperture area against pad area. What is it?

options.text: 40 % to 60 % of the pad area, to leave room for the fillet to form
100 % to 120 % of the pad area, to supply the fillet and the standoff
20 % to 40 % of the pad area, because chip joints need very little paste
80 % to 100 % of the pad area, with less for the smallest chips

explanation: The lesson gives 80 % to 100 % of pad area as a common starting point for many chip sizes, with reduced area for the smallest components to avoid tombstoning and bridging. The other bands are outside the guidance, and going above the pad area works against the rule that the aperture stays within the pad.

prompt: For a 0.4 mm pitch QFP the lesson reduces a 0.25 mm by 0.60 mm land to a 0.22 mm by 0.55 mm aperture in 0.10 mm foil. What area ratio results?
explanation: Area = 0.22 x 0.55 = 0.121 mm²; perimeter = 2 x (0.22 + 0.55) = 1.54 mm; sidewall = 1.54 x 0.10 = 0.154 mm²; area ratio = 0.121 / 0.154 = 0.786. The 0.68 answer uses the full land instead of the reduced aperture, 0.86 forgets one pair of sides in the perimeter, and 1.10 treats the aspect ratio as the answer.

prompt: Why are BGA apertures usually made smaller than the ball diameter?

options.text: To leave clearance so the ball can self-centre on the land during placement.
To control paste volume and keep the ball from collapsing unevenly at reflow.
To keep the aperture inside the solder mask opening rather than the copper land.
To reduce the area ratio so that paste releases more slowly onto the land.

explanation: The lesson ties BGA aperture geometry to pitch, ball diameter and paste collapse, with apertures smaller than the ball to control volume. Self-centring comes from the reflow forces, not from paste clearance; the aperture is set against the land and mask design, not in place of it; and a lower area ratio is a cost of the choice, not its purpose.

prompt: A mixed board carries 0402 chips, a 0.4 mm pitch QFP and a large thermal pad. Which stencil decision does the lesson support?

options.text: Thick base foil for the thermal pad, with aperture reduction on the fine pitch to compensate.
Uniform mid-thickness foil, since the worst case on the board sets a single workable value.
Thin base foil for the fine pitch, with a local thick step for the thermal pad.
Two separate stencils, because one foil cannot carry features of such different scale.

explanation: This is the case the step stencil exists for: the fine pitch needs a thin foil to keep the area ratio and control bridging, the thermal pad needs volume, and the step supplies both locally. A thick base foil cannot be rescued by aperture reduction on fine pitch, a mid value fails both extremes, and two stencils multiply the print operations for no process gain.

prompt: Which geometry choice does the lesson map to preventing tombstoning of small chips?

options.text: Increasing the aperture area above the pad so each end gets generous paste.
Using the thickest available foil so the deposit stands proud of the pad.
Opening the centre pad in one piece so the chip sits flat during reflow.
Reducing aperture area on the smallest chips so each end gets balanced paste.

explanation: The lesson lists reduced aperture area for the smallest chips among the measures against tombstoning and bridging, because unbalanced or excessive paste at the two terminations drives the chip up. More paste, thicker foil and a single large opening all move in the wrong direction.

prompt: Which wall taper does the lesson cite as the recommended band?

options.text: 85 to 90 degrees measured from the horizontal plane
60 to 75 degrees measured from the horizontal plane
75 to 85 degrees measured from the vertical plane
90 to 105 degrees measured from the horizontal plane

explanation: The lesson gives 85 to 90 degrees from the horizontal plane, noting that a slight taper reduces the effective wall area and so helps release. A very aggressive taper changes the effective aperture at the top and bottom of the foil, which is why the band is narrow and why the reference plane matters when the value is quoted.

prompt: A drawing review finds that the specification states an area ratio requirement but not the measurement method. What should the reviewer do?

options.text: Accept the drawing, since area ratio is a design value that needs no measurement method.
Require the method and sample size to be defined before the stencil is fabricated.
Delete the area ratio requirement, because an unmeasurable requirement cannot be enforced.
Ask the supplier to choose a method and to report the result with the finished stencil.

explanation: The lesson asks the reviewer to confirm that the measurement method and sample size in the supplier specification are sufficient to verify what the drawing requires — so an undefined method is a gap to close before fabrication. A design value still has to be verified on the delivered part, deleting the requirement removes the control, and delegating the choice to the supplier leaves the acceptance basis undefined.

prompt: A drawing specifies a 0.30 mm square aperture in 0.120 mm foil, with a issued minimum area ratio of 0.66. What do the nominal figures show?

options.text: Area ratio 0.625, above the issued minimum, so the aperture passes as drawn
Area ratio 0.750, above the issued minimum, so the aperture passes as drawn
Area ratio 0.625, below the issued minimum, so the aperture fails as drawn
Area ratio 2.500, above the issued minimum, so the aperture passes as drawn

explanation: Area = 0.09 mm²; perimeter = 1.20 mm; sidewall = 1.20 x 0.120 = 0.144 mm²; area ratio = 0.09 / 0.144 = 0.625. That is below the issued minimum of 0.66, so the drawing fails its own requirement — the case the lesson works through. The 0.750 answer drops one side of the perimeter, and 2.500 is the aspect ratio.

prompt: What does the aperture calculator exist to do before fabrication?

options.text: Produce the final aperture drawing so the designer does not have to place apertures.
Estimate the cost of the stencil from the aperture count and the foil thickness.
Set the printer recipe, including squeegee pressure and separation speed, for the product.
Turn pad geometry, foil thickness and wall condition into ratios and volume for review.

explanation: The calculator converts the design inputs into release metrics that can be reviewed before the foil is cut, so a release problem is found on paper. It does not replace the drawing, its output is not a cost model, and printer settings are established separately on the machine with the actual paste.

prompt: A measured value sits below the guidance value but inside the issued specification tolerance. Which basis governs acceptance?

options.text: The issued specification governs; the guidance value is reviewed with engineering.
The guidance value governs, because it comes from the design reference standard.
Neither: a value inside tolerance is accepted without further review by definition.
The lower of the two values always governs, so the part is rejected in every case.

explanation: The lesson is explicit that acceptance compares the measured value against the issued specification rather than against a general guideline, and that a value outside the issued tolerance needs a disposition. Guidance values inform the review, they do not override the contract, and accepting silently on tolerance alone or rejecting automatically are both wrong readings of the same sentence.

prompt: Which item list belongs in a stencil drawing review before fabrication?

options.text: Printer brand, squeegee material, paste lot number and the production schedule of the line.
Aperture sizes and tolerances, foil thickness, wall taper, fiducials, step features.
Panel quantity, freight terms, supplier payment terms and the packing method for shipment.
Reflow profile zones, oven chain speed and the cooling rate used downstream of printing.

explanation: The lesson lists aperture dimensions, tolerances, foil thickness, wall taper, fiducials, aperture-to-pad alignment, step features and the paste assumptions as the review content. Printer, paste-lot and schedule data are process inputs reviewed elsewhere; commercial terms and reflow settings are not stencil drawing content.

prompt: What makes a stencil measurement report usable as an acceptance record?

options.text: It states that the stencil was measured and found to meet the supplier specification.
It lists the aperture count and the foil grade, which are the only fixed characteristics.
It names the drawing revision, method, operator, date and serial number of the stencil.
It is signed by the supplier quality manager, which makes the values contractually valid.

explanation: The lesson requires the report to be traceable — drawing revision, measurement method, operator, date and serial number — so that a value can be tied to the part and reproduced. A general statement of conformity, a partial list of characteristics or a managerial signature does not let the buyer verify each reported value against the issued specification.

prompt: On what basis does the lesson say a stencil should be retired?

options.text: A fixed number of print cycles, because wear is predictable from the fabrication method.
The expiry date printed on the frame label by the stencil manufacturer at delivery.
The number of cleaning cycles only, since cleaning is what wears the aperture walls.
Measured drift, repeated print defects or a failed inspection, not a cycle count alone.

explanation: The lesson asks for the lifetime record to track print cycles, paste exposure, cleaning cycles and method, inspection findings, tension, thickness, aperture wear and step condition, and states that retirement follows measured drift, repeat defects or a failed inspection rather than a cycle count alone. Cleaning is one contributor, not the single criterion, and frames do not carry a wear-out date.

prompt: Issued: foil 0.120 mm ±0.010 mm, aperture width 0.400 mm ±0.025 mm, area ratio at least 0.66. The report gives thickness 0.128 mm, width 0.418 mm and area ratio 0.64. What is the acceptance result?

options.text: Thickness and width pass; area ratio fails, so the stencil is rejected or dispositioned
Thickness and width pass; the area ratio is close enough, so the stencil is accepted
The width fails because 0.418 mm is outside the 0.375 to 0.425 mm band
The thickness fails because 0.128 mm is outside the 0.110 to 0.130 mm band

explanation: Thickness limits are 0.110 to 0.130 mm, so 0.128 passes; width limits are 0.375 to 0.425 mm, so 0.418 passes; the area ratio of 0.64 is below the issued minimum of 0.66, so the stencil fails on that characteristic and needs rejection or an engineering disposition. Two of the distractors assert failures on values that are inside their bands.

prompt: Why does the lesson treat a delivered stencil as a controlled part rather than as a consumable?

options.text: It is expensive, so it has to be tracked by the finance system as a fixed asset.
Its geometry sets paste volume, and that has to be verified against a drawing revision.
It is reused across products, so its history has to follow it between work orders.
It is supplied by an external vendor, so it falls under purchasing rather than production.

explanation: Control follows from function: the stencil decides deposit volume, so its dimensions, taper, tension and step depth are verified against a named drawing revision and tracked through its working life. Cost accounting, cross-product reuse and vendor ownership are administrative facts that do not explain why the geometry needs an acceptance record.

prompt: Appearance of insufficient paste on one fine-pitch area began after the third cleaning of a stencil. What should be checked first?

options.text: The paste lot and its viscosity, then the reflow profile of the product.
The board surface finish, then the solder mask registration across the panel.
Aperture condition and wall damage from cleaning, then the print settings.
The squeegee hardness, then the ambient humidity of the print room that shift.

explanation: The lesson ties low area ratio, poor wall taper and damaged walls to paste left in the aperture, and it requires the cleaning regime to be verified and the apertures inspected after cleaning. A change that follows a specific cleaning cycle points at the aperture and the wall; paste, profile, finish, squeegee and humidity are all worth reviewing later but none of them explains the timing.

prompt: A stencil specification is silent on flatness. What does the lesson direct you to do?

options.text: Accept any flatness, because an unstated requirement cannot be enforced at receipt.
Reject the drawing until the customer adds a flatness limit to the specification.
Apply the foil thickness tolerance to flatness, since both are dimensional features.
Use the design reference and agree a documented range with the supplier.

explanation: The lesson says that where the specification is silent, use the design reference such as IPC-7525C and the paste or equipment datasheet, and set a documented range with the supplier using the supplier's measurement method. Accepting anything, blocking the drawing or borrowing an unrelated tolerance all leave contact across the print area uncontrolled.

prompt: What does an area reduction against the pad actually buy on a fine-pitch print?

options.text: Less paste per pad and more room between deposits, so bridging risk falls
A higher area ratio, because a smaller opening always releases paste better
A thicker deposit, because the same paste volume is pushed into less area
A stronger stencil wall, since the aperture becomes narrower at the top

explanation: Reduction trades paste volume for separation: each deposit is smaller and the gap to the neighbouring aperture grows, which is why it is used where slump or smear could bridge. A smaller opening lowers the area ratio rather than raising it, the deposit follows the foil thickness rather than growing taller, and wall strength is a fabrication property, not a consequence of reducing the opening.

prompt: A 0.30 mm square pad gets a 10 % area reduction and is printed through 0.12 mm foil. The area ratio falls short of the release target. What is the right correction?

options.text: Reduce the aperture further, since a smaller opening releases paste faster
Reduce the foil thickness so the wall area shrinks and the ratio rises
Raise the squeegee pressure until the aperture fills despite the geometry
Increase the paste metal load so the deposit holds its shape after release

explanation: The lesson's remedy for a low area ratio is to specify a thinner foil that meets the release target while keeping the paste volume practical: sidewall area is perimeter times thickness, so thinning the foil raises the ratio. Shrinking the aperture further lowers it, pressure cannot repair a wall-dominated release, and metal load affects slump rather than the geometry ratio.

prompt: A 0.30 mm square pad is reduced by 10 % in area and printed through 0.12 mm foil. What area ratio results, and what does it mean?

options.text: 0.59, above the 0.66 release guideline, so the aperture releases cleanly
0.74, below the 0.66 release guideline, so the aperture must be enlarged
0.59, below the 0.66 release guideline, so the foil must be reconsidered
1.19, above the 0.66 release guideline, so the print is comfortable

explanation: Aperture area = 0.081 mm², side = 0.285 mm, perimeter = 1.14 mm, sidewall = 1.14 x 0.12 = 0.1368 mm², so area ratio = 0.081 / 0.1368 = 0.592. That is under the 0.66 guideline, which is exactly the situation the lesson resolves with a thinner foil. The 0.74 answer forgets the perimeter of the reduced square, and 1.19 uses the pad area rather than the reduced aperture.

prompt: Which quantity does a stencil's area ratio tell you about the paste?

options.text: How much solder the joint needs once the paste has reflowed
How far the paste spreads sideways after the stencil lifts
How accurately the aperture is registered to the pad centre
How strongly the walls hold the deposit back as it leaves

explanation: Area ratio compares the opening to the wall area the paste must slide past, so it predicts release. The joint requirement comes from the volume budget, lateral spreading is slump, and aperture-to-pad alignment is registration — three different checks the lesson keeps separate from the ratio.

prompt: The same aperture prints well at 0.10 mm foil and poorly at 0.15 mm foil. What explains it?

options.text: The sidewall area grew with the foil, so the area ratio dropped
The paste volume grew with the foil, so the joint became over-filled
The aperture area shrank as the foil thickened, so less paste was released
The paste had less time to fill a deeper aperture at the same print speed

explanation: The aperture footprint is unchanged, but the sidewall band around it grows with thickness, so the area ratio falls and release suffers — the trade the lesson describes between volume and release. The joint being over-filled is a consequence at reflow rather than the printing mechanism, the aperture area does not shrink with foil thickness, and fill time is a separate effect that would not by itself explain the change.

prompt: A 0.25 mm square aperture is cut in 0.12 mm foil. What are the area ratio and the aspect ratio?

options.text: Area ratio 0.52, aspect ratio 1.5
Area ratio 0.52, aspect ratio 2.1
Area ratio 0.65, aspect ratio 2.1
Area ratio 2.10, aspect ratio 0.52

explanation: Area = 0.0625 mm²; perimeter = 1.0 mm; sidewall = 0.12 mm²; area ratio = 0.52. Aspect ratio = 0.25 / 0.12 = 2.08. The 0.65 answer divides by twice the sidewall, the 1.5 answer copies the guidance figure instead of computing, and the last option swaps the two results.

prompt: Why does the lesson treat volume as the primary SPI metric rather than height or area alone?

options.text: Volume is the only metric the machine can measure without a calibration step
Volume is insensitive to stencil thickness, so it compares across all products
Volume combines area and height, so it tracks solder available to the joint
Volume is the only metric that correlates with how cleanly the paste released

explanation: Volume is the product of the printed area and the printed height, which is why it maps most directly onto the solder available after reflow. Height and area are still needed, because they explain why the volume moved; the machine calibrates all of them; and the volume depends directly on stencil thickness rather than being independent of it.

prompt: Which pattern points to a clogged aperture rather than to poor release?

options.text: Low height together with a normal area, spread across the whole panel
Normal height with a high area, concentrated at the panel edges
High volume with a small offset, appearing after a stencil wipe
Low height together with a low area, on one aperture class only

explanation: A clog reduces the open area as well as the deposit, so both height and area fall. Low height with normal area is the incomplete-fill or release signature, and the lesson gives high volume with a small offset as a different combination. Concentration on a single aperture class is the clue that the geometry, not the printer, is at fault.

prompt: An aperture of 0.080 mm² is printed through 0.120 mm foil, and the volume window is set at 80 % to 120 % of nominal. What are the limits?

options.text: 0.00768 to 0.01152 mm³ around a nominal of 0.0096 mm³
0.00640 to 0.00960 mm³ around a nominal of 0.0096 mm³
0.00768 to 0.00960 mm³ around a nominal of 0.0080 mm³
0.00800 to 0.01200 mm³ around a nominal of 0.0100 mm³

explanation: Nominal = 0.080 x 0.120 = 0.0096 mm³, so the window is 0.8 x 0.0096 = 0.00768 and 1.2 x 0.0096 = 0.01152 mm³. The second option applies the 80 % limit twice, the third takes the aperture area as the nominal volume, and the fourth invents a nominal of 0.0100 mm³ instead of deriving it.

prompt: How does a process window differ from a set of control limits?

options.text: The window comes from the customer; the limits come from the standard
The window makes a good joint; the limits describe your spread
The window is fixed per product; the limits are the same for every line
The window is the machine specification; the limits are the SPI threshold

explanation: The process window is the range of SPI values that yields acceptable joints for that product and process, while control limits describe stable variation calculated from your own data once special causes are removed. Limits are therefore line-specific, and neither is a customer document, a machine specification or an SPI threshold.

prompt: Volume dips by 15 % for one board and recovers on the next. What is the sound first reading?

options.text: Common-cause variation, so the process should be left alone and monitored
A paste lot change, because only a lot change moves volume that far
A special cause such as a wipe or a manual intervention, not a drift
A calibration error, because SPI cannot measure a single board reliably

explanation: The lesson separates isolated spikes and short runs, which usually follow a change such as a stencil wipe, from the stable band of common-cause spread and from step changes after a lot change. A single board that recovers is the spike case, so neither monitoring nor blaming calibration is the first move.

prompt: An SPI report gives a printed area of 0.120 mm² and a printed height of 0.100 mm, against a nominal of 0.0096 mm³. What is the printed volume as a percentage of nominal?
explanation: Printed volume = 0.120 x 0.100 = 0.0120 mm³; as a percentage of 0.0096 that is 125 %. The 80 % answer takes the height alone as a fraction of the stencil thickness, 12.5 % misplaces a decimal, and 105 % adds the two ratios instead of multiplying the measurements.

prompt: What does the lesson say about treating squeegee pressure, speed, snap-off, separation and wipe as separate knobs?

options.text: They are coupled, so change one at a time and inspect the deposit each time
They are independent, so they can be optimised in parallel to save setup time
They are ranked, so pressure is tuned first and the rest are left at default
They are machine constants, so only the paste supplier may propose new values

explanation: The lesson opens by calling printer setup a coupled process: the settings control paste roll, aperture fill, release and residue together, so the method is one variable at a time with the deposit inspected and the direction of the change predicted beforehand. Treating them as independent or as fixed machine constants removes the ability to attribute any effect.

prompt: Prints show paste bleed under the stencil and bridging between adjacent pads. Which direction of change does the lesson predict?

options.text: Increase squeegee pressure and reduce the wipe frequency to keep the roll wet
Reduce squeegee pressure and address speed, separation and underside residue
Increase snap-off speed so the stencil lifts clear before the paste can spread
Increase separation so the paste roll has more room to move ahead of the blade

explanation: The lesson maps bleed and bridging to excessive pressure, and it lists reducing pressure, adjusting speed, checking separation and cleaning the stencil underside as the coupled response. More pressure drives paste under the foil, faster snap-off pulls tails rather than preventing bleed, and excess separation pushes the roll ahead of the blade instead of settling it.

prompt: A 250 mm blade is loaded with 125 N against a recommended 0.8 to 1.2 N/mm. What force range does that recommend for this blade?

options.text: 100 N to 150 N, against a current 0.5 N/mm
125 N to 188 N, against a current 0.5 N/mm
200 N to 300 N, against a current 0.5 N/mm
800 N to 1200 N, against a current 5.0 N/mm

explanation: 0.8 x 250 = 200 N and 1.2 x 250 = 300 N, so the current 125 N is 0.5 N/mm and sits below the band. The 100-150 N answer applies the band to the force rather than to the per-length value, 125-188 N divides instead of multiplying, and 800-1200 N treats the blade length as 1000 mm.

prompt: What is snap-off, in the lesson's terms?

options.text: The gap between the stencil and the board before the squeegee starts moving
The frequency with which the underside of the stencil is wiped during a run
The angle of the squeegee blade relative to the direction of the print stroke
The controlled lift-off after the stroke that frees paste from the walls

explanation: Snap-off is the controlled lift-off after the print stroke, and both too fast and too slow versions cause faults: tails and pulled paste at one extreme, smearing at the other. The pre-stroke gap is separation, wipe frequency is the wipe cycle, and blade angle is a different setup parameter.

prompt: Apertures are underfilled on small openings only, while large pads print well. Which setting is the lesson's first suspect?

options.text: Squeegee pressure at the low end, which leaves small apertures short of fill
Wipe frequency at the high end, which removes paste from the aperture walls
Separation at the low end, which keeps the roll from reaching the small pads
Snap-off speed at the low end, which lets the stencil drag across the board

explanation: The lesson states that low pressure leaves apertures underfilled, especially on small apertures and high aspect-ratio stencils, which matches a size-dependent pattern. Excessive wiping would show as drying and clogging across classes, a small separation leaves the roll pushed ahead rather than short of fill on small openings, and a slow snap-off smears instead of starving small apertures.

prompt: Insufficient paste persists after pressure is corrected. What is the next single change the lesson lists?

options.text: Increase print speed so the paste is sheared harder at the aperture mouth
Reduce print speed so the apertures have more time to fill
Increase separation so the paste roll is pushed further ahead of the blade
Reduce wipe frequency so more paste remains on the stencil underside

explanation: The lesson's sequence for insufficient paste is pressure within range first, then reducing speed when fill time is the limiting factor, then separation and wipe frequency. Raising speed reduces fill time, a larger separation pushes the roll away from the apertures, and leaving residue on the underside adds bleed rather than fill.

prompt: What is thixotropy, in the lesson's description of paste behaviour?

options.text: The fall in viscosity with temperature, which lets paste flow into apertures
The metal fraction of the paste by weight, which sets the deposit volume
The recovery of viscosity after shear, which lets the deposit hold its shape
The resistance of the flux to oxidation while the paste sits on the stencil

explanation: Thixotropy is shear thinning followed by recovery: the paste must flow while the squeegee works it and then stiffen again so the deposit keeps its shape, and slow recovery is one cause of slump. Temperature dependence, metal load and flux oxidation are separate properties with their own effects on the print.

prompt: Volume falls steadily through a shift while the printer settings never change. Which explanation fits the lesson?

options.text: The stencil is wearing thinner, so each aperture now holds less volume
The squeegee is softening with use, so it pushes paste less effectively
The SPI is drifting out of calibration, so the readings fall without cause
Paste on the stencil is drying and thickening, so it releases less readily

explanation: The lesson names solvent evaporation, temperature rise and repeated rolling as the changes that make paste on the stencil print lower volume later in a shift — the paste-life effect. Stencil wear over a shift is not a thickness change of that size, squeegee softening is a wear trend over many cycles, and a calibration drift would have to be demonstrated before it displaces the process explanation.

prompt: A 0.40 mm square aperture in 0.12 mm foil prints with a mean height of 0.085 mm and a mean area of 0.145 mm². What volume percentage does that give?

options.text: 64 %, which matches a low-height, low-area release pattern
88 %, which matches a low-height, normal-area release pattern
71 %, which matches a normal-height, high-area pattern
118 %, which matches an excess-paste pattern

explanation: Nominal volume = 0.16 mm² x 0.12 = 0.0192 mm³; printed volume = 0.145 x 0.085 = 0.012325 mm³; percentage = 64.2 %. The 88 % answer uses the mean area as a percentage of nominal area, 71 % mixes height and area ratios, and 118 % inverts the division.

prompt: What does slump look like on an SPI report?

options.text: A smaller area with a higher height, as the deposit pulls back together
A larger area with lower height, as deposit flows out after release
Normal area and height with a large offset from the pad centre
High volume on a single pad that appears immediately after a wipe

explanation: Slump is lateral flow after release, which spreads the footprint while the height falls. Pulling back into a taller smaller deposit is the opposite change, a large offset with normal dimensions is a placement or registration symptom, and a single high-volume pad after a wipe is a special cause rather than slump.

prompt: Volume is low while the printed area is high. Which pair of causes does the lesson put together?

options.text: Incomplete fill or poor release, where the aperture never filled
Stencil-to-board misregistration, where deposits land off centre
Slump or bleed, where the paste spreads instead of standing up
Excess paste, where too much material was pushed through the opening

explanation: Low volume with high area is the spreading signature: the paste covers more of the pad while standing lower, which is slump or bleed. Incomplete fill and poor release give low area as well, misregistration shows up as offset, and excess paste raises the volume rather than lowering it.

prompt: A paste with a nominal density of 1.0 prints a deposit of 0.0144 mm³ into an aperture whose nominal volume is 0.0192 mm³. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The printed volume is 133 % of nominal, above the target band
The printed volume is 75 % of nominal, inside the target band
The printed volume cannot be compared without the metal load figure
The printed volume is 75 % of nominal, below the target band

explanation: 0.0144 / 0.0192 = 0.75, so the deposit is 75 % of nominal — below the 80-120 % band the module uses as a working window. The 133 % answer inverts the division, the second 75 % answer mis-states where the band lies, and the comparison needs the geometric nominal volume, which is given; density cancels in the ratio.

prompt: What does Cp measure that Cpk does not?

options.text: Whether the spread would fit if centred, ignoring where the mean sits
Whether the mean is off centre, taking the specification limits into account
Whether the process is stable over time, before any capability is calculated
Whether the specification limits themselves are set at a realistic width

explanation: Cp compares the specification width with the process spread and assumes the process is centred; Cpk adds the distance from the mean to the nearer limit. Stability is a precondition for either figure rather than a component of them, and neither says anything about whether the limits were set correctly.

prompt: What does the lesson conclude when the trend is stable but the process is off centre?

options.text: Stop the line, because a centred process cannot be recovered by tuning
Adjust the print parameters that control transfer, then re-measure
Widen the specification limits so the existing mean becomes acceptable
Recalculate the capability figure using the run mean instead of the target

explanation: A stable but off-centre process is the case the lesson treats with parameter adjustment: paste temperature, pressure, speed, snap-off and separation, followed by measurement. Stopping is for instability, widening the limits changes the requirement rather than the process, and substituting the run mean hides the offset that Cpk exists to expose.

prompt: Paste volume has a mean of 92 %, a standard deviation of 6 %, and specification limits of 85 % and 115 %. What are Cp and Cpk?

options.text: Cp 0.83 and Cpk 1.28, so the spread is too wide but the process is centred
Cp 1.43 and Cpk 0.39, so the spread is acceptable but the process is low
Cp 0.83 and Cpk 0.39, so the spread is too wide and the process is low
Cp 2.50 and Cpk 1.28, so both the spread and the centring are acceptable

explanation: Process spread = 6 x 6 = 36 points, so Cp = 30 / 36 = 0.83. The nearer limit is the lower one, 92 - 85 = 7 points, and 7 / 18 = 0.39 for Cpk. The 1.28 figure is the distance to the upper limit, the 1.43 comes from dividing by two standard deviations, and 2.50 uses a single standard deviation as the spread.

prompt: What does a wide histogram on an SPI report tell you before any limit is set?

options.text: The print is centred, because a wide histogram must straddle the target
The print is acceptable, because the mean is the only quantity that counts
The SPI is misconfigured, because a healthy process gives a single bar
The print is inconsistent, so the distribution matters more than the mean

explanation: A narrow peak near target is the healthy shape; a wide distribution signals inconsistency from paste temperature, cleaning variation, squeegee wear or board support. Width says nothing about centring, a good mean can hide a bad spread, and a real process never reports a single-valued bar.

prompt: Volume steps down and stays down from one board onward. Before touching the printer, what does the lesson have you check?

options.text: What changed there: paste lot, stencil, blade, tension, calibration
The long-term trend, because a step is the same thing as a slow drift
The specification limits, because a step means the window was too tight
The operator, because a step can only come from a manual intervention

explanation: The lesson separates step changes, which point at a discrete event such as a lot, stencil, blade, tension or calibration change, from gradual drift, which points at something wearing or drying. A step is not a drift, the limits did not move, and a manual intervention is only one of the candidate events rather than the only one.

prompt: A process has a mean of 100 %, a standard deviation of 8 % and limits of 85 % and 115 %. What is its Cpk?
explanation: The nearer limit is 15 points away, and three standard deviations is 24 points, so Cpk = 15 / 24 = 0.63. The 1.88 answer divides the specification width by the standard deviation, 0.42 uses five standard deviations, and 3.75 takes the half-width over a single standard deviation.

prompt: Which combination of SPI readings argues for under-fill rather than smearing?

options.text: Low volume, low height but a high area on the affected deposits
Low volume with a normal height and a large offset from centre
Low volume, low height and low area on the affected deposits
High volume with a high area across the whole panel

explanation: Under-fill means less paste went in, so all three dimensions fall together. Low height with a high area is the spreading pattern of smear or slump, an offset with normal dimensions is a registration problem, and high volume with high area is excess.

prompt: Offset appears on a few pads at the same panel location, board after board. What does the lesson point to?

options.text: Paste rheology, because slump would show up as a consistent offset
Aperture geometry, because a small aperture shifts the deposit sideways
Stencil thickness, because a thicker foil moves paste away from the pad
Board support, conveyor handling or vision registration there

explanation: The lesson links a repeating offset at one location to support, conveyor handling or vision registration rather than to the paste, because a positional pattern needs a positional cause. Rheology changes the deposit shape, aperture geometry changes its size, and foil thickness changes its volume — none of them moves deposits in one direction at one place.

prompt: Mean volume is 82 % of nominal, mean height is 0.11 mm against a 0.12 mm nominal, and mean area is 95 % of nominal. Which dominant defect mode does that pattern name?

options.text: Under-fill, because volume and height are down with the area nearly intact
Smearing, because the area is slightly below nominal and the height is low
Excess paste, because the volume percentage is well inside the window
A registration error, because offset is the only metric that explains this

explanation: The lesson reads this triple as insufficient transfer: volume at 82 % and height below the foil thickness, with the area close to nominal, which rules out the spreading pattern where area rises. Smearing would raise the area, excess would raise the volume, and the offset in the case is small enough not to explain a volume loss of that size.

prompt: Why is an SPI report more than a pass/fail screen?

options.text: It certifies that the joints will meet the workmanship standard
It measures how much, where and how consistently paste was deposited
It replaces the first-article inspection of the printed board
It records the operator, the shift and the paste lot for traceability

explanation: The lesson frames SPI as a measurement of quantity, position and consistency, whose value is the diagnostic pattern across metrics, histograms and trends. SPI measures paste, not reflowed joints; it does not replace first-article inspection; and traceability data is recorded elsewhere.

prompt: Volume is low on every board of the run, never recovering. What does the lesson distinguish this from?

options.text: A false SPI call, where the machine misreads a sound deposit
A special cause, where one board falls outside the stable band
A drifting process, where the loss grows board by board
A design change, where the aperture was revised between runs

explanation: A stable low-volume trend from the first board is a design or setup issue — aperture, thickness, paste rheology — while a gradual downward drift is a wearing or drying process. Both are real defects, the distinction decides where you look first; a false call and a single outlier are different cases again, and a design change would show as a step.

prompt: Bridging appears between adjacent fine-pitch pads with high area between them. Which geometry change does the lesson map to it?

options.text: Aperture too small for the pitch, so the paste spreads to reach the joint
Foil too thin for the pitch, so the paste cannot stand on the pad
Wall taper too steep, so the deposit lands off the centre of the pad
Aperture too large for the pitch, so the wall holds no paste back

explanation: The lesson maps adjoining pads joined by paste to an aperture that is too large for the pitch, which is why area reduction and thinner foil are the countermeasures on fine pitch. A smaller aperture starves the joint instead of spreading, foil thickness affects volume and release rather than lateral reach, and wall taper affects release, not deposit position.

prompt: What does the lesson require before any printer setting is changed?

options.text: Confirm the defect is repeatable and not an SPI artifact
Confirm the paste lot is fresh and the stencil below its cycle limit
Confirm the specification limits were agreed with the customer
Confirm the operator has completed the printer training record

explanation: Triage comes first: establish that the defect repeats and that it is real rather than a threshold, lighting, focus, fiducial or residue artefact, then record the baseline conditions. Freshness, cycle counts, agreed limits and training are legitimate controls, but none of them substitutes for proving the defect exists.

prompt: A single-variable experiment shows no response to any printer setting. What does the lesson say to do next?

options.text: Widen the specification limits so the current output becomes acceptable
Look at stencil and paste together: area ratio, walls, thickness
Change several settings at once to move the process further in one step
Replace the printer, because a no-response result proves the machine is at fault

explanation: The lesson says that when a single-variable experiment shows no response, the stencil and paste interaction is the next place to look, because small apertures with a low area ratio or rough sidewalls release poorly even at reasonable settings. Widening limits changes the requirement, changing several variables destroys attribution, and a no-response result is evidence about the geometry rather than a verdict on the machine.

prompt: A 1.0 mm by 0.5 mm aperture in 0.10 mm foil prints 0.035 mm³ against a theoretical 0.050 mm³. What fill factor is reached, and what does the target require?

options.text: 70 % now against an 80 % target, so the process already meets the window
143 % now, because the theoretical volume is smaller than the measured one
70 % now against a 90 % target, so transfer must improve by a fifth
35 % now against a 90 % target, so the aperture must double in area

explanation: Aperture area = 0.50 mm², theoretical volume = 0.050 mm³, so the current fill is 0.035 / 0.050 = 70 % and the 0.045 mm³ target needs 90 %. The 80 % answer uses the wrong band, 143 % inverts the ratio, and 35 % divides by the wrong nominal.

prompt: What makes an SPI reading an artifact rather than a real print defect?

options.text: It repeats on every board and on every aperture class in the panel
It persists after the stencil has been cleaned and the paste replaced
It appears in the trend chart as a steady band around the target
It comes from a threshold, lighting, focus or residue effect

explanation: The lesson lists threshold settings, lighting, focus, fiducial errors, board warp, paste colour, solder mask variation and stencil residue as artefact sources, and asks for confirmation by manual inspection, paste weight, cross-section or repeatability. Repeating after cleaning and appearing as a stable band are properties of real process behaviour, not of artefacts.

prompt: Which experiment plan does the lesson describe for a print problem?

options.text: Fix the metric and baseline, change one variable, run enough boards
Change the three most likely settings together and compare the mean volume
Run one board per setting, since SPI measures every pad on the panel
Run the experiment on a scrap panel with the production paste lot replaced

explanation: The lesson asks for a defined defect, baseline settings and acceptance metric, a stable lot and clean stencil, then one variable changed at a time, with roughly 10 boards and 30 measured deposits per condition. Changing several together loses attribution, a single board cannot separate effect from noise, and substituting the paste lot adds a second change.

prompt: Small apertures print low volume although pressure and speed are in range. Which starter change does the lesson list?

options.text: Increase wipe frequency to keep the small apertures free of residue
Increase snap-off distance to improve release from the small openings
Reduce paste metal load so the paste flows into the smaller openings
Reduce separation so the stencil sits closer to the board during printing

explanation: The lesson says that increasing snap-off distance often improves release for small apertures and warns that too little separation drags paste and leaves it in the stencil. Wiping more helps residue rather than release, metal load is a paste formulation decision, and reducing separation works against release.

prompt: A machine hits the same wrong spot on every board. Which property is at fault?

options.text: Accuracy: the commanded position does not match the true board location
Repeatability: the machine cannot return to the same point twice in a row
Throughput: the placement cycle is longer than the programmed time
Nozzle vacuum: the component slips in the nozzle after the pick

explanation: Consistent arrival at the wrong coordinate is the definition the lesson gives for an accuracy fault: repeatable but inaccurate, corrected by calibration and compensation. Poor repeatability shows up as scatter around a point, throughput does not move a coordinate, and vacuum loss would produce tilted or dropped parts rather than a constant offset.

prompt: Which set does the lesson say to verify before a production run starts?

options.text: Purchase orders, supplier invoices, reel prices and the delivery schedule
BOM, library, nozzle map, feeder setup, coordinates and calibration
Reflow zones, conveyor speed, paste lot and the stencil tension record
Operator certifications, shift plan, machine warranty and spare-parts stock

explanation: The lesson lists the BOM, library, nozzle map, feeder setup, pick and place coordinates, rotation, skip logic, vision settings, support and calibration status as the pre-production checks, followed by a dry cycle or first article. Paste, stencil and reflow belong to the print and reflow stages, and the remaining items are commercial or staffing data.

prompt: A 1.0 mm by 0.5 mm chip with a 0.30 N force limit is picked with a 0.30 mm nozzle at a vacuum pressure of 400 hPa. What is the force on the component face?

options.text: About 2.83 N, which would exceed the limit by an order of magnitude
About 0.07 N, which is far below the limit and risks a dropped part
About 0.28 N, inside the limit but with little margin
About 0.50 N, which equals the component mass limit for the part

explanation: Tip area = π x (0.15)² = 0.0707 mm² = 7.07 x 10⁻⁸ m², and 400 hPa = 4 x 10⁴ Pa, so the force is about 2.8 x 10⁻³ N — expressed at the component scale in the lesson as roughly 0.28 of the 0.30 N allowance. The 2.83 N answer forgets that the area is in square millimetres, 0.07 N confuses the area figure with a force, and 0.50 N is the limit of the neighbouring 0402 case.

prompt: What does placement control deliver to the reflow stage?

options.text: A guaranteed solder joint, because placement force seats the termination
The paste volume under each lead, which placement sets by the force applied
The final electrical connection, verified by the placement vision system
The initial position of every component, to be held or corrected by solder

explanation: The lesson describes placement as transferring components and setting the initial position before reflow; the joint is formed later, and solder can only correct a limited error. Paste volume comes from the print, and electrical continuity is a test-stage question.

prompt: A machine passes a capability check on a bare test coupon but places off-centre on product boards. What does the lesson point to?

options.text: Board recognition and support, since the product panel is not the coupon
The vacuum nozzle, because a worn tip shows only on production material
The paste lot, because a fresh paste pulls components sideways at placement
The machine throughput, because higher speed reduces the settling time

explanation: A difference between coupon and product performance points at what changed — board recognition, support and fiducials on the real panel — rather than at the machine axes, which the coupon already exercised. A worn nozzle and paste rheology can shift parts, but neither is specific to product boards, and speed is a separate variable the lesson treats under throughput.

prompt: An axis calibration certificate expired three weeks ago and production has continued. What is the correct position?

options.text: The setup stands, because three weeks is inside the typical grace period
The setup is not verified; complete or repeat calibration before release
Only future work is affected, so the lots already built can be released
Calibration matters for accuracy only, so repeatability data can close the gap

explanation: The lesson treats a missing or expired calibration certificate as a verification gap that blocks release, which is the case worked in m05l05. There is no grace period in the lesson, already-built lots cannot be declared sound on an unverified machine, and the accuracy-repeatability distinction does not make one of them optional.

prompt: What goes wrong when pick height is set too low?

options.text: The vacuum does not seal, so the part is missed or picked at an angle
The component is lifted too high and released before the board is reached
The nozzle pushes into the pocket, distorting tape or cracking parts
The feeder advances twice, because the pocket sensor is triggered early

explanation: Too low seats the nozzle into the component and the pocket, which distorts tape and can crack brittle ceramics. A poor vacuum seal is the too-high failure, and the lesson does not describe double-advance or premature release as pick-height defects.

prompt: A 0402 MLCC with a 0.5 N supplier limit shows corner cracks after placement. What is the first check?

options.text: The reflow profile, because thermal ramp is the usual cause of corner cracks
The solder mask thickness, because a raised mask tilts the part on contact
The feeder pitch, because the wrong pitch drops the part onto the board
Nozzle tip and placement force: point loading or a worn tip cracks ceramics

explanation: The lesson warns that small ceramic capacitors can crack under point loading, especially with a worn or misaligned tip, and that force must stay below the supplier maximum with margin. The reflow ramp, the mask and the feeder advance cause other signatures, and none of them loads a corner of the body.

prompt: An 0402 part has a 0.5 mm body height and sits in a tape pocket 0.8 mm deep, so its top is 0.3 mm below the tape surface. What does that imply for the pick height?

options.text: The nozzle must travel 0.3 mm deeper than the tape surface to reach the part
The nozzle must stop 0.3 mm above the tape surface to avoid the pocket walls
Pick height is unaffected, because the machine references the pocket floor
The pocket cannot be used, because a part set below the surface cannot be picked

explanation: 0.8 - 0.5 = 0.3 mm is the gap between the tape surface and the component top, so the pick position has to account for it — the arithmetic of the lesson's 0402 case. The other options either avoid the component, assume a datum the lesson does not state, or reject a perfectly normal tape-and-reel arrangement.

prompt: Which three inputs does the lesson use to choose a nozzle for a part?

options.text: Tape width, reel diameter and the feeder slot number
Top surface geometry, mass and height of the part
Paste volume, pad area and the stencil thickness
Machine brand, head type and the vacuum pump capacity

explanation: Nozzle choice follows the component: the shape of the top surface it must seal against, the mass it must hold and the height it must reach over. Tape and reel data belong to feeder setup, paste and stencil data to printing, and machine data constrains the choice without defining it.

prompt: Complaints of occasional tilted placements appear on one feeder only. Which evidence separates nozzle wear from tape pocket problems?

options.text: Increase the placement force on that feeder until the tilt stops
Replace the paste lot, because tilt is usually a rheology symptom
Swap the nozzle to another head and see if the tilt follows
Reduce the machine speed across the line and compare the run totals

explanation: A component that is attached to one head and leaves its symptom behind when it is moved implicates the nozzle; a symptom that stays on the feeder implicates the tape. Raising force treats the symptom and risks cracking parts, paste rheology does not select a feeder, and a line-wide speed change destroys attribution.

prompt: How does the lesson want a new nozzle, pick height and force combination to be confirmed?

options.text: Start from the previous product settings and adjust only if defects appear
Start at the machine maximum and reduce until parts stop breaking
Start from the paste datasheet recommendation and keep the nozzle unchanged
Start from supplier limits, run a sample, inspect it, then release

explanation: The lesson asks for a controlled trial: component supplier limits first, then a small sample inspected for missed picks, tilt and damage, then release. Carrying over another product's settings, running at the maximum and working backward, or taking the value from the paste datasheet all skip the validation step.

prompt: Why does the lesson insist that a placement offset is a vector rather than a distance?

options.text: The direction separates a coordinate error from a mechanical shift
The distance alone cannot be compared with the tolerance in the drawing
The vector is the only form the placement machine can report to the operator
The distance would be identical for every component on the same panel

explanation: Two offsets of the same magnitude in different directions have different causes, so direction is diagnostic — which is why a single scalar hides the mechanism. The magnitude is exactly what gets compared with the tolerance, the machine can report either form, and offsets do vary across a panel.

prompt: A component is centred correctly but its body is rotated relative to the pads. What is that, and what does the lesson compare it with?

options.text: Offset, compared with the X and Y distance from the programme target
Skew, compared with the angle and the offset between opposite ends
Tilt, compared with the Z shadow and focus of the body on the pad
A wrong part, compared with the BOM and the expected electrical value

explanation: A correctly centred but rotated body is skew, and the lesson measures it either as an angle error or as an asymmetric offset between opposite ends of the component. Offset moves the centre, tilt is out of plane in Z, and a wrong part is a different component entirely.

prompt: A part targeted at X = 120.000 mm, Y = 80.000 mm is measured at X = 120.045 mm, Y = 79.985 mm, with a 0.05 mm tolerance. What is the total offset?

options.text: 0.060 mm, outside the 0.05 mm tolerance
0.030 mm, inside the 0.05 mm tolerance
0.047 mm, inside the 0.05 mm tolerance
0.047 mm, outside the 0.05 mm tolerance

explanation: ΔX = +0.045 mm and ΔY = −0.015 mm, so the magnitude is √(0.045² + 0.015²) = 0.0474 mm, inside the 0.05 mm limit. The 0.060 answer adds the two components, and 0.030 takes only the smaller axis — both errors that a scalar reading of the offset invites.

prompt: What is the role of a global fiducial in placement?

options.text: It marks the polarity of the component nearest to it on the panel
It sets the paste deposit height reference for the print stage
It marks the position of the panel on the conveyor for the operator
It locates the board so the machine works in board coordinates

explanation: Global fiducials on the board edges or panel let the vision system find the board and map the programme coordinates onto it. Polarity is a component marking, paste height is a print measurement, and the conveyor position is handled by the machine rather than by a fiducial.

prompt: Offset grows towards one corner of the panel and is near zero at the opposite corner. What mechanism does that pattern suggest?

options.text: Vision scale or registration, which accumulates across the panel
A worn nozzle, which affects every component equally on the panel
Paste slump, which increases with time since the panel was printed
A feeder misload, which places one part type at the wrong coordinate

explanation: An error that scales with distance from a reference is a registration or scale effect, which is why the lesson treats vision calibration as part of the coordinate chain. A worn nozzle, a feeder misload and paste slump do not produce a smooth position-dependent gradient across the panel.

prompt: Which programme check does the lesson ask for beyond part numbers?

options.text: That the part numbers in the programme match the purchase order of the build
That the origin, fiducial pattern and panel offsets match the design
That the operator has entered the reel barcodes before the run starts
That the machine clock is synchronised with the plant MES server

explanation: The lesson wants programme verification to test geometry — coordinate origin, fiducial pattern, panel offsets, mirroring, units, side and layer — and not only the part list. Barcode capture and clock synchronisation are traceability controls, and matching part numbers to the order is the part-list check, not the geometry check.

prompt: Which evidence sequence does the lesson prescribe before naming a mechanism?

options.text: The final AOI image alone, since it shows the defect as the customer sees it
The operator report, since only the operator saw the machine at the time
SPI paste data, pre-reflow AOI, head and feeder logs, then reflow and final
The supplier datasheet, since the component defines its own placement limit

explanation: The lesson opens by rejecting a visual guess: the sequence is paste print, pre-reflow placement, then post-reflow evidence, correlated with feeder slot, nozzle id and profile. A single final image cannot separate print from placement from reflow, and neither an operator report nor a datasheet substitutes for the chain.

prompt: Ten of twelve large offsets occur at the same feeder slot. What does the lesson attribute that to?

options.text: Camera calibration drift, which would affect the whole panel evenly
Reflow profile imbalance across the board, which tilts parts outward
A programme coordinate error, which would hit every part equally
Feeder pickup offset or tape pocket deformation at that slot

explanation: The lesson states that systematic defects by feeder slot point to feeder loading, pickup offset or tape condition at that slot. A calibration drift and a coordinate error are not slot-specific, and reflow acts after placement rather than at one feeder.

prompt: In a 5,000-board run, AOI finds 26 placement defects, of which 12 are offset. What are the total and offset rates in ppm?

options.text: 5,200 ppm total and 2,400 ppm offset
520 ppm total and 240 ppm offset
5,200 ppm total and 4,333 ppm offset
26 ppm total and 12 ppm offset

explanation: 26 / 5,000 x 10⁶ = 5,200 ppm and 12 / 5,000 x 10⁶ = 2,400 ppm. The 520 and 240 answers divide by 10⁵ instead of 10⁶, 4,333 ppm divides the defect count by 12 rather than by the board count, and 26 ppm omits the million-scaling entirely.

prompt: How does the lesson distinguish a tombstone from a tilt?

options.text: A tombstone is a horizontal rotation, while a tilt is a vertical offset
A tombstone is a severe tilt, one end lifted and the other still wetted
A tombstone is a missing part, while a tilt is a part placed off centre
A tombstone is a wrong part, while a tilt is a part placed upside down

explanation: Tilt is a non-coplanar body, and a tombstone is the extreme case where one termination lifts clear while the other remains soldered. Rotation is skew, absence is missing, and a reversed part is a polarity defect — three separate families in the same atlas.

prompt: The component sits exactly where the paste was printed, but the paste itself is off the land. Which stage owns the defect?

options.text: Placement, because the component must be centred on the land regardless
Reflow, because the paste can only move once it has melted
Printing, because the placement followed the paste rather than the land
Stencil design, because an aperture offset can only be a design error

explanation: The lesson gives this as the discriminator: if the component follows the paste, the print is the source. Placement centring on paste is normal behaviour rather than a fault, paste does not migrate before reflow, and an aperture offset is one possible cause inside the printing stage rather than a separate stage.

prompt: A polarized diode is reversed on a single board. Which check does the lesson put first?

options.text: The reflow profile, because uneven heating rotates the body at melt
The nozzle vacuum, because lost vacuum spins the part in flight
The paste volume, because excess paste floats the part and turns it
Feeder orientation and the tape pocket orientation for that part

explanation: The lesson lists feeder orientation, tape pocket orientation, manual loading, a disabled polarity vision check and nozzle rotation among the causes, and the feeder and tape are the first physical checks. Reflow, vacuum loss and paste volume produce other signatures, and none of them reliably turns a part through 180 degrees.

prompt: What does the component library hold that a BOM does not?

options.text: Geometry, rotation, pick point, nozzle, feeder type and vision settings
The purchase price, the supplier and the lead time for each component
The electrical value, tolerance and voltage rating of each component
The reflow profile and the peak temperature the component can survive

explanation: The library is what turns a part number into machine instructions: geometry, pitch, polarity, rotation, pick point, nozzle, feeder type, vision settings and placement tolerance. Price and lead time are commercial, electrical values and thermal ratings belong to the part specification rather than the placement library.

prompt: Which change forces the pre-production verification to be repeated?

options.text: A change of operator on the same machine with the same programme loaded
A change of programme, library, feeder, nozzle, panel or calibration
A change of shift pattern while the same product stays on the line
A change of packaging for the outgoing finished boards at dispatch

explanation: The lesson ties re-verification to anything that can move a coordinate or change a pickup: programme, library, feeder, nozzle, panel, fiducial or calibration status. Operators, shift patterns and dispatch packaging change, but none of them alters what the machine was verified to do.

prompt: A programme allows 0.05 mm centre deviation, the sample measures 0.03 mm, and the calibration certificate is missing. What is the release decision?

options.text: Release: the measured deviation is inside the 0.05 mm tolerance
Release with a note: the missing certificate can be closed after the run
No release: the measurement passes but the calibration is unverified
Reject the product: a deviation of 0.03 mm is 60 % of the tolerance

explanation: This is the lesson case: 0.03 mm is inside tolerance, but a missing calibration certificate means the setup is not verified, so release is refused until calibration is completed and the sample repeated. Passing the dimensional check does not override an unverified measurement chain, and 0.03 mm is comfortably acceptable, so rejecting the product is wrong in the other direction.

prompt: Why must acceptance criteria exist before the pre-production sample is run?

options.text: Otherwise the machine cannot select the correct nozzle for the sample
Otherwise the sample cannot be measured, because no method is defined
Otherwise the calibration certificate cannot be issued before the run
Otherwise the sample result cannot decide anything, only get rationalised

explanation: The lesson asks for pass and fail criteria to be defined first, covering coordinate tolerance, polarity, rotation, missing or wrong components and calibration status, because a result judged after the fact is judged against the result. Criteria do not select nozzles, define a measurement method, or issue certificates.

prompt: The feeder map in the programme no longer matches the physical feeders. What does the lesson predict?

options.text: Wrong-part or missing defects: the machine picks from the wrong lane
A uniform offset, because the coordinate origin has moved on the panel
Polarity errors only, because lane mapping affects only orientation
No effect, because the machine re-reads feeder barcodes before each pick

explanation: A feeder map is the mapping between programme slots and physical lanes, so a mismatch means the head picks a different part from the one the programme expects — the wrong-part and missing family. It does not move the coordinate origin, it is not limited to orientation, and the lesson does not assume an automatic barcode check at the pick.

prompt: Which records does the lesson want stored with the release?

options.text: The machine purchase invoice, warranty terms and the service contract dates
Programme and library versions, calibration records, sample results
The operator roster, shift plan and the training certificates of the line
The customer order number, delivery date and the agreed inspection level

explanation: The lesson asks for the programme version, library version, calibration records, sample results and approvals, so a later change or defect can be traced to the setup that was released. Commercial, staffing and order data belong to other records.

prompt: Why does a 0.5 mm pitch QFP expose placement errors so clearly?

options.text: The package is heavier than most parts, so it settles under its own mass
The leads are longer than on coarser packages, so they bend more easily
The allowed positional margin is small compared with the lead pitch
The body is larger, so any rotation error displaces the leads less

explanation: The lesson notes that on a 0.5 mm pitch a lateral shift of 0.10 mm already uses a fifth of the available margin, so the same machine error that is invisible on a coarse package shows up here. Mass, lead length and body size work in the other direction or are not the mechanism the lesson describes.

prompt: Defect rate on a QFP is high on the first boards after each stencil wipe. Which stage does the lesson expect?

options.text: Placement, because the machine restarts its cycle after each wipe
Reflow, because the oven door opening disturbs the profile briefly
Depanel, because panel stress releases position errors at singulation
Printing: the paste deposit changed and the component followed it

explanation: The lesson's discriminator is whether the component follows the paste: a defect that clusters after a wipe points at the deposit that the wipe disturbed. Placement does not reset on a stencil wipe, and reflow and depanel defects have different patterns and different timings.

prompt: A QFP with a 14.0 mm body diagonal shows X = +0.08 mm and Y = −0.06 mm offset, against a limit of ±0.10 mm. What is the resultant offset?

options.text: 0.10 mm, exactly at the machine limit, so it is borderline
0.14 mm, above the machine limit and therefore a rejection
0.07 mm, comfortably inside the machine limit
0.02 mm, inside the limit with a large margin

explanation: √(0.08² + 0.06²) = 0.10 mm exactly, so the part sits on its capability limit and the lesson calls for investigation rather than a clean pass. The 0.14 answer adds the components, 0.07 takes the mean, and 0.02 takes the difference.

prompt: How do offset and skew differ on a fine-pitch QFP?

options.text: Offset is measured in degrees; skew is measured in millimetres from the pads
Offset moves the centre; skew puts one side closer to its pads
Offset affects the leads; skew affects only the body outline and its marking
Offset is a placement fault; skew is always produced later by reflow forces

explanation: The lesson separates translation of the centre from a positional mismatch between opposite sides, and notes that one side being closer than the other is the visible sign of skew. The units in the second option are inverted, skew is a placement measurement too, and the body outline is not what is being measured.

prompt: Missing QFPs appear at random positions across many boards. Which mechanism does the lesson name first?

options.text: Camera calibration drift, which shifts every part by the same amount
Paste slump, which lets the part slide off the pad after placement
Feeder, vision or cycle failures rather than a process drift
Reflow voids, which lift the package away from the pads at melt

explanation: Random missing parts point to discrete failures — empty feeder, pick failure, vacuum loss, vision reject, skipped programme entry — rather than to a gradual shift, which is what the lesson contrasts. Calibration drift is systematic, and slump and voids act after the part is already on the board.

prompt: Rotation is +0.8° on a package whose corner is 7.0 mm from the centre. What displacement does that rotation cause at the corner?

options.text: About 0.098 µm
About 5.6 mm
About 0.014 mm
About 0.098 mm

explanation: 0.8° = 0.01396 rad, and 7.0 x 0.01396 = 0.0977 mm — nearly the whole 0.10 mm budget, which is why rotation matters on a fine pitch. The second option confuses the unit scale, the third multiplies the radius by the angle in degrees, and the fourth uses a sin approximation with the wrong angle.

prompt: Why is an oven setpoint not evidence that the solder joint reached its target?

options.text: The board and joint lag the air, and mass and copper pull the joint colder
The oven setpoint is measured in the exhaust, which runs hotter than the board
The setpoint is an average across all zones, so it cannot describe any one zone
The setpoint is calibrated in the factory and never verified again after that

explanation: The profile is the temperature history of the board and components, and board thickness, copper area, component mass and mounting all make the joint differ from the air around it — which is why thermocouples go on the board. The setpoint is a control target per zone, not an exhaust reading, not an average, and not a static factory value.

prompt: What is the job of the soak zone?

options.text: To melt the solder quickly so the joint spends as little time hot as possible
To let the assembly even out thermally while flux activates and solvents leave
To cool the board gradually so that thermal stress does not build in the joints
To burn off the flux residue before the solder reaches its liquidus

explanation: The soak brings heavy planes and small pads towards a common temperature while flux works and volatiles escape, which is what prevents violent boiling in the ramp. Melting is the reflow zone, cooling follows the peak, and flux is not burned off before liquidus — its activity is what the reflow window depends on.

prompt: A 1.6 mm board ramps from 25 °C to 150 °C in 60 s. What is the ramp rate, and how does it compare with the 1-3 °C/s guidance?

options.text: 2.5 °C/s, inside the guidance band
0.5 °C/s, below the guidance band
2.1 °C/s, inside the guidance band
2.1 °C/s, above the guidance band

explanation: (150 - 25) / 60 = 2.08 °C/s, which sits inside 1-3 °C/s. The 2.5 answer divides by 50 s for no stated reason, 0.5 inverts the division, and the last option reads the same number against the wrong side of the band.

prompt: Which quantities describe a reflow profile?

options.text: Zone count, belt speed, heater power and blower frequency
Paste metal load, powder size, flux type and viscosity
Board thickness, copper weight, panel size and fixture type
Ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak and cooling

explanation: The lesson defines a profile by those five thermal features measured at the board. Machine settings are how you produce the profile rather than the profile itself, and paste and board data are the constraints the profile has to satisfy.

prompt: A profile logged on a thin coupon passes, but the same recipe makes cold joints on the heavy product board. What is the first explanation?

options.text: The coupon did not reproduce the board thermal mass, so joints ran colder
The oven lost calibration between the coupon run and the production run
The paste lot changed between the two runs, raising the liquidus temperature
The belt speed was recorded in the wrong units on the production recipe

explanation: The lesson requires a test coupon that reproduces the laminate, copper distribution, components and panel position, precisely because a thinner, lighter coupon heats differently. Calibration, a paste lot and a unit error are all possible, but the systematic difference between coupon and product is the first thing the evidence points at.

prompt: Cooling runs from 240 °C to 180 °C in 20 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: 3 °C/s, above the 1-4 °C/s typical band
3 °C/s, inside the 1-4 °C/s typical band
12 °C/s, far above the typical band
1 °C/s, at the bottom of the typical band

explanation: (240 - 180) / 20 = 3 °C/s, inside 1-4 °C/s. The 12 °C/s answer divides the temperature span by the number of zones instead of by seconds, and 1 °C/s mis-divides by 60.

prompt: What happens when the ramp from room temperature is too steep?

options.text: The flux is consumed too early, so the joints come out dull but sound
The intermetallic layer grows too thick before the solder even melts
Trapped solvent boils violently, producing solder balls and spatter
The board cools faster afterwards, which coarsens the grain structure

explanation: A steep ramp outgasses solvent faster than the paste can release it, which is the balling and spatter mechanism the lesson describes. Flux activity, intermetallic growth and cooling rate are all influenced by the profile, but their effects come from other segments and in other directions.

prompt: From which temperature is time above liquidus measured for SAC305?

options.text: 217 °C, the solidus, since melting begins there
183 °C, the eutectic SnPb liquidus, used as a common reference
250 °C, the classification temperature for the package size
219 °C, the liquidus, not the 217 °C solidus

explanation: SAC305 melts over a two-degree range, and the lesson measures TAL from the 219 °C liquidus because that is where the alloy is fully molten and free to flow. The solidus marks the start of melting, 183 °C belongs to SnPb, and the classification temperature is a ceiling rather than a reference for the clock.

prompt: A profile measures 248 °C peak against a J-STD-020 classification of 245 °C for the package, and 100 s above liquidus against a 60-150 s window. What is the critical finding?

options.text: The peak exceeds the classification temperature by 3 °C
The time above liquidus is the critical finding, since 100 s is inside 60-150 s
Both values are acceptable, because 3 °C is inside measurement uncertainty
Both values are unacceptable, because the window and the ceiling are both missed

explanation: The TAL sits comfortably inside its window, so the finding that matters is the peak exceeding the component classification by 3 °C — the lesson treats the classification temperature as a ceiling, not a target. Calling the TAL critical inverts the finding, and dismissing the overshoot as uncertainty assumes a measurement error the profile does not show.

prompt: What does the reflow zone have to achieve before the joint can form?

options.text: A peak high enough to melt the laminate surface so the pad is exposed
Enough time above liquidus for wetting and oxide removal, not more
A soak long enough that the paste is fully dried before it melts
A cooling rate fast enough to freeze the joint before it can re-oxidise

explanation: TAL has to be long enough for wetting and flux action and short enough to limit intermetallic growth and component exposure — a two-sided requirement. Melting laminate, drying paste before melting and relying on fast cooling to prevent oxidation all describe different processes than the one the lesson sets out.

prompt: Joints on a heavy ground plane are cold while small pads nearby are perfect. Which segment does the lesson fix first?

options.text: The peak, raised until the plane joints finally melt and wet
The cooling, slowed so the plane joints have time to solidify evenly
The soak, so the plane reaches temperature before the reflow zone
The ramp, steepened so the plane gets more heat in less time

explanation: The lesson assigns soak problems to non-wetting and cold joints in heavy copper areas, because the soak is where the assembly is equalised. Raising the peak to force the plane up also over-heats everything else, cooling acts after the joint has formed, and a steeper ramp risks the solvent and spatter problems without equalising anything.

prompt: A joint is above 219 °C from 240 s to 305 s. How long is the time above liquidus, and does it sit in the 60-150 s window?

options.text: 305 s, inside the window
65 s, outside the window
55 s, below the window
65 s, inside the window

explanation: 305 - 240 = 65 s, which is above the 60 s floor, so it sits inside 60-150 s. Reading the end time as the duration and mis-subtracting to 55 s are the two arithmetic slips this question is designed to catch.

prompt: Which measurement does a thermal survey have to report to be useful?

options.text: The coolest and the hottest joint, not the average of the two
The average board temperature across the whole run of panels
The oven air temperature in each zone and the exhaust temperature
The peak reading of the logger, since that is the worst case on the board

explanation: The decision rule is built on two ends: the coolest joint must reach liquidus with enough TAL, and the hottest must stay below the component and board limits. An average hides both ends, and zone or exhaust air temperatures are control targets rather than what the joints experience.

prompt: Where does the lesson expect the coolest site on a panel to be?

options.text: At the centre of the panel, where the conveyor clamps hold the board most rigidly
Under a large ground plane, at a cold edge, under a heavy part or in poor airflow
On the smallest chip, because it has the least thermal mass to retain heat
At the leading edge, because it meets the coldest air in each zone first

explanation: The lesson names the ground plane, the cold edge, the heavy component and the poorly supplied position as candidate cold sites, and the inverse for hot sites near a heater or a small component with less mass. Panel centre, smallest chip and leading edge all point the other way.

prompt: A survey records a coolest peak of 238 °C and a hottest peak of 246 °C, against a liquidus of 219 °C. What margin does the coolest joint have above liquidus?
explanation: 238 - 219 = 19 °C, which is the margin the lesson checks against the paste and component limits. The 27 °C answer uses the hottest peak, 21 °C measures from the 217 °C solidus, and 8 °C is the spread between the two thermocouples rather than a margin above liquidus.

prompt: Why does the lesson require the test coupon to reproduce the production board?

options.text: A coupon is only a carrier for thermocouples and its material is irrelevant
The coupon is required by the standard to be a bare laminate of the same size
A coupon must carry the same component count but may use any laminate available
